notes.AS04: The passage shows Jacob tearing his clothes and mourning his son for many days, refusing to be comforted by his children. It speaks to grief that will not be eased, which the passage presents as lasting and hard to console. It says nothing about a parent who was unkind or about guilt, so it fits only the mourning part of what you describe.
notes.AS06: The passage speaks of regret settling on the narrator as their mother disappears, and of tears that come too late to change anything. It does not speak to relief, so it fits the regret you describe but not the relief or the feeling of being a monster. The passage says the parting had already happened before the tears came.
notes.AS07: The passage speaks to being with a grieving person in conversation: it says to accommodate yourself to them and, if need be, to groan with them. It also says not to be overcome by the apparent evil, because what hurts is the view a person takes of an event. It does not say how often to check in or whether to give space, so it does not answer that question.
notes.AS12: The passage speaks to feeling lonelier among people than alone. It says that company, even the best, soon wears a person down, and that solitude is not measured by distance. It speaks to the loneliness you feel beside him, but it does not say whether this relationship is right for you.
notes.AS14: The passage speaks to resentment toward someone who has wronged you. It says resentment can be let go by thinking, in effect, that they did wrong but there is nothing one can do. The passage does not address checking his accounts, blocking him, or the waiting you describe.
notes.AS16: The passage speaks of a brother's injustice and says it can be carried by one handle and not by the other. It says to take hold of the wrong by the fact of kinship and shared upbringing rather than by the injustice itself. It speaks to the blame you describe only in that way and does not mention favouritism, shouting, or the label of attention seeking.
notes.AS20: The passage speaks to the family's wishes. It says to forget your own interests for theirs, even when nature rebels, and to take some burden upon yourself to ease others. It does not address the move abroad, and it speaks from a faith that the passage presents as its own counsel.
notes.AS21: The passage speaks to how much of a life is woven from others: its clothes, meals and beds all belong to other people. It asks how a person can separate themselves from others, which speaks to the sense of owing your family everything. It does not speak to moving out, to what your mother will face, or to how independence is reached.
notes.AS28: The passage is a lament in which the speaker says friends have been taken away and turned from them, and that their eyes are dim from grief. It speaks to the hurt of being left out by friends, which is what your girlfriend's distress describes. It does not speak to how to help her or what to say, so it fits only the grief and not your question.
notes.AS30: The passage speaks to how a person's own words should be used: left unsaid when false or useless, and spoken at the right time when true and helpful. It does not speak to being criticised in public or to the choice between staying and leaving. It fits the question of speech, not the experience you describe.
notes.AS34: The passage speaks to holding on to what you have while trying to leave. It says that a person who keeps looking back to count what to take will never get free, and that no one can swim ashore carrying their baggage. It does not speak to income, family needs, or how people manage without a job.
notes.AS39: The passage speaks to money as a source of toil and tears. It says that possessions bring worry in proportion to gain, and that losses hurt more than they should. It describes the anxiety you mention about money, but it does not speak to debt, budgeting, or whether your efforts are working.
notes.AS45: The passage speaks to fear and to the counting of failures: it says not to be afraid and not to count how many times one has failed, because time is endless. It says to keep going and keep asserting oneself, and that light must come. It does not speak to the medical news itself, to his reaction, or to whether you can face this a second time.
notes.AS57: The passage speaks to a wish to end one's life that was held back by thinking of a loved one's grief. It says that living can itself take courage. It does not speak to forgiveness, to the affair, or to whether you deserve to feel alive.
notes.AS58: The passage speaks to betrayal by a trusted friend who shared bread with the speaker. It describes the hurt of that betrayal and mentions no fault on the speaker's side. It does not speak to whether you encouraged what happened, so it does not answer the question you ask about yourself.
notes.AS61: The passage says Abram was told to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house for a land he would be shown. It speaks to leaving home on a command, which is a faith story. It does not speak to your family, your job, or whether relocating is the right choice for the long run.
notes.AS63: The passage speaks to the gap between how a person appears and how they feel inside. It says to be content to be thought foolish about external matters, and to distrust yourself when others regard you as important. It speaks to the fear of being seen through, but it does not say whether that fear is accurate or what would change it.
notes.AS66: The passage speaks to a longing for God that has gone quiet. It describes the heart crying out for light and for a sense of God's presence, in moments of great dejection, and says the next moment such thoughts are forgotten. It does not speak to prayer or worship, and it does not say what is missing.
notes.AS69: The passage speaks to how one's view of things can be renewed. It says principles survive when the thoughts behind them are kept alive, that outside things have no hold on the mind, and that life can be recovered by looking at things again as one once did. It speaks to the change in how your work feels, but not to the accident itself or to everyday routines.
notes.AS76: The passage says a person whose dart has been drawn out lies down unafraid and full of sympathy for all living creatures. It speaks to the peace of sleep and to kindness toward living things, which fits the calm moment you describe. It does not speak to the dog or to the adoption itself.
notes.H03: The passage speaks to the part of your words about plans and the future: the sense that the life you had arranged has been cut off, and that the hopes of your heart have gone with it. It says nothing about who was at fault or how to judge the anger, so it does not answer those questions. Its words are a lament over what has been broken off, and they stay with that loss.
notes.H06: The passage speaks to the part of your words about this one closed door. It says that young people lose heart when a first undertaking fails, and that someone who tries many paths has a hundred chances, not one. It does not speak to the years of work or the dream itself, and it makes no promise about which path will open.
notes.H07: This passage describes a grief close to yours: after the loss of a close friend, the writer says everything he saw was death, home became a torment, and the places they shared were unbearable without him. It speaks to how the loss runs through every place and habit. The friend in the passage is a person, so it fits the emptiness more than anything about the dog itself, and it says nothing about what comes after.
notes.H08: The passage speaks to one part of what you wrote: the worry that children can become either a justification or a regret. It is a single line, so it does not speak to the choice between your career and your time with them, and it does not suggest which to give up or how to share your time.
notes.H10: The passage speaks to one part of what you describe: how you hold on to what your mother does. It suggests, using a brother as its example, taking hold of the bond rather than the hurt. It does not speak to the twisting of your words, the guilt, or whether there is a way out of the cycle you describe.
notes.H12: The passage speaks to the isolation you describe: it says that cutting yourself off makes everything hurt. It suggests that feeling for others brings help. It does not speak to the attempts that ended badly, and it says nothing about finding someone to talk to.
notes.H14: The passage speaks to the part of your words about your friend and the cost of revealing his secrets. The passage says a wound can be bound up and a quarrel made up, but that one who reveals secrets has lost hope. It does not speak to the wife or to what silence would mean for her.
notes.H15: The passage speaks to one part of what you wrote: being belittled at work and kept at one level. It says that the rank of a job does not make the person lower, and that people are judged by the spirit they bring to their work. It does not speak to your boss's conduct, to credit being taken, or to the job-market worries that keep you where you are.
notes.H16: The passage speaks to the sense that time has gone and that what you wanted may not have come. Its writer, in old age, says he has stopped wanting what he wanted as a boy, and that he treats each day as if it were a complete life. It does not say whether your goals are still reachable, and it does not argue with the sense of having fallen short.
notes.H18: The passage speaks to the question of what all the running is for. It says that this world is a means and not the end, and that people forget this and take this life as the goal. It answers only in that direction and does not say what the means lead to. The passage says this from a faith in a life beyond this one, and it does not present that belief as proven.
notes.H19: The passage says that crying out about how dark a room is does not make it lighter, and that bringing in light is what removes darkness. It speaks to the way you describe the world's darkness, but it names no particular light. It does not speak to the war, cruelty or poverty themselves, or to how the darkness creeps in.
notes.H20: The passage says that outward religious practice matters less than whether a person practises the virtues and gives their will over to God's will. It speaks from a faith you say you do not practise, so it cannot settle whether a shared religion matters, whether going along with it would be pretence, or what the two of you may decide.
notes.H21: The passage speaks to the shock of being betrayed by a friend you trusted and shared a table with, which matches the way you say this has shaken you. It does not speak to the friend's reasons, to your message to your ex, or to what happens with your boyfriend.
notes.H22: The passage speaks to your question of whether leaving would be enough. It says that the falseness is outside the church as well, and that the lie can be found in one's own manners and speech. It does not say whether to stay or go, and it does not speak to the morality you describe as lacking in the church.
notes.H24: The passage speaks to the link between thought and the body's look: it says sour thoughts make a sour face, and that malice and despondency rob the body of its grace. It does not speak to how you look or to the dread you describe each morning. It is not a claim that your feelings are a fault of your thinking.
notes.H25: The passage speaks to the weight you have struggled with: it says that what one dreads losing is measured by one's own standard, and that others would not blink at losing what they have. It is about judging other people by one's own measure, so it does not speak to how you judge yourself. It does not speak to the comment that hurt you or to the eating.
notes.H28: The passage speaks to the part of your words about how you raised him: it says that deciding for a child from outside, without seeing things from where he stands, will not be obeyed. It does not say how to restore contact, and it does not speak to the guilt you carry.
notes.H29: The passage speaks to how one takes it when others get what one hoped for. It suggests rejoicing in another's good, and not grieving over a missed gain if the thing itself is bad. It does not speak to your wife's reaction, or to the grudge you suspect her of.
notes.H30: The passage says that poverty is an event, and that calling it evil is an opinion added to it. It suggests that the harm lies in that opinion, not in the poverty itself. It does not speak to the money you have now or to the hurt and anger you describe, and it does not say those feelings are wrong.
notes.H32: The passage speaks to the years of waiting, and to the feeling that a quiet moment was what had been waited for. It describes a simple exchange of smiles and small talk, not a grand event. It does not speak to the engagement, the future, or whether this is the happiest day.
